title: Eggs and cholesterol: what the relationship actually means

seo.title: Eggs and cholesterol: what the evidence means
seo.meta_description: One large egg has roughly 185–200 mg cholesterol, almost all in the yolk. That does not translate directly into the LDL number on a blood test.
seo.search_intent: Understand how much cholesterol eggs contain, how eggs can affect blood cholesterol, and what current U.S. guidance says.

excerpt: A large egg contains roughly 185–200 mg of dietary cholesterol, almost all in the yolk; the white contains essentially none. Dietary cholesterol can affect LDL, but the milligrams in an egg do not translate directly into the number on a blood test because the liver regulates cholesterol metabolism and people respond differently. Current American Heart Association guidance places more emphasis on the overall dietary pattern and saturated fat than on dietary cholesterol alone; its egg-specific advisory says healthy people can include up to one whole egg a day.
content_html:
Eggs have one feature that explains decades of conflicting headlines: the yolk is high in dietary cholesterol but relatively low in saturated fat. That makes an egg a poor fit for the old shortcut that treated every cholesterol-rich food as if it affected blood cholesterol in the same way.

How much cholesterol is in an egg?

A large egg provides roughly 185–200 mg of cholesterol, with essentially all of it in the yolk. The white is mostly water and protein and contains negligible cholesterol.

The same egg supplies about 6–7 g of protein, around 5 g of total fat and roughly 1.5–2 g of saturated fat. That combination—high dietary cholesterol but modest saturated fat—matters when interpreting the food.

Eating 200 mg does not add 200 mg to your blood

Only part of dietary cholesterol is absorbed. At the same time, the liver makes cholesterol and adjusts its own production and clearance. Two people eating the same egg intake can therefore have different changes in LDL.

Genetics, baseline lipid levels, the rest of the diet and other metabolic factors all contribute. There is no reliable one-to-one equation between yolks eaten and LDL points gained.

The saturated fat around the egg can matter more

An egg contains substantial cholesterol but only about 1.5–2 g of saturated fat. Bacon, butter, sausage or full-fat cheese can add much more saturated fat to the same breakfast.

That is why an egg served with vegetables, beans, whole-grain toast and unsaturated fat is a different dietary pattern from eggs routinely paired with processed meats and butter. The American Heart Association's 2026 dietary guidance says dietary cholesterol is no longer a primary target for most people and emphasizes replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat within an overall heart-healthy pattern.

What current U.S. guidance says about eggs

The AHA's dietary-cholesterol science advisory states that healthy individuals can include up to one whole egg per day as part of a healthy dietary pattern. That is not a requirement to eat an egg every day, and it comes with caveats for people with dyslipidemia and certain other cardiovascular risk conditions.

The broader 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans emphasize whole, nutrient-dense foods and limiting sources of saturated fat rather than treating dietary cholesterol as a stand-alone daily score.

If LDL is already high, the question becomes more individual

High LDL, familial hypercholesterolemia, established cardiovascular disease, diabetes and other risk factors can change the balance. In those settings, dietary cholesterol may deserve more attention alongside saturated fat and other lifestyle and medical treatment goals.

A general population recommendation should not be used as a personal cholesterol-treatment plan.

Yolk and white are not nutritionally interchangeable

Egg whites can add protein without adding the yolk's cholesterol. But removing every yolk also removes choline and much of the egg's fat-soluble vitamins and other micronutrients.

Combining one whole egg with extra whites is one practical way to raise protein while limiting additional dietary cholesterol, but it is a different nutritional choice rather than a perfect substitute for whole eggs.

The useful takeaway

Eggs really are high in dietary cholesterol, but that number alone does not predict your LDL. The amount eaten, individual response and the rest of the dietary pattern all matter. For healthy U.S. adults, the AHA's egg-specific guidance allows up to one whole egg per day within a heart-healthy pattern.

faq.question: How much cholesterol is in one egg?
faq.answer: A large egg typically contains roughly 185–200 mg of dietary cholesterol, almost all of it in the yolk.

faq.question: Do egg whites contain cholesterol?
faq.answer: They contain essentially none. Egg white is mostly water and protein; the yolk contains the cholesterol.

faq.question: Can healthy people eat an egg every day?
faq.answer: The American Heart Association's dietary-cholesterol advisory says healthy individuals can include up to one whole egg per day within a healthy dietary pattern.
